brief.arc: Single email, single movement: name what is now available in the terms of the thing this reader was already planning to build, show the two structural differences that matter to someone who has read the build guides (no vector store to run; every Slack answer lands as an inspectable run), and ask for one narrow test — one document set, one channel — rather than a decision.
brief.sequence_rationale: The contract is one email, so the whole argument has to be carried by the claim with the best odds of landing cold on a solution_aware reader. Three candidates were live. Price was rejected outright: five competitors make the same free-tier and cheap-tier argument, the company's own pricing pages contradict each other on Pro's limits, and an email quoting a plan number invites the reader to find the contradiction. Integration breadth was rejected because the positioning read puts the field ahead of us on breadth and explicitly says not to invite that comparison — and because this reader needs exactly one channel, Slack, which is a verified native integration. That leaves the run record, which is the only open ground in the competitive read and, not coincidentally, the gap this audience names in their own published accounts of the low-code stack they use today: it works, and it tells them nothing. So the email leads on "configure it, and then you can see what it did" and spends its evidence on Slack as a native channel, retrieval with no vector database to maintain, and analytics that arrive without extra configuration. Objections deliberately left unassigned because the evidence cannot beat them: the SOC 2 report does not exist (in progress only), SSO is Enterprise-only, and "we already pay for a workspace AI assistant — why a third thing" has no answer anywhere in the material. None of these are hinted at or written around; the email simply does not open a vendor-evaluation conversation, and asks for a side-by-side test on one document set instead of a switch. The one thing you could send us that would most change this campaign: which customers or quotes may we name? Proof is the empty shelf here — there is not a single customer name, usage number or testimonial in the entire corpus, so every email this business sends is the company asserting things about itself, and one nameable customer running a Slack bot on their handbook would be worth more than any rewrite of this brief.
